instagram_caption:
🚀 The AI Chip Squeeze: how NVIDIA went from “GPU company” to the AI powerhouse while Intel got cornered.

It starts in the mid‑2010s. In 2015, NVIDIA is a niche giant with about **$6.5B** in sales moving through the ecosystem, while Intel sits at roughly **$54B**—the default “everything-chip” authority. AMD is small but growing (about **$4.0B**), and Qualcomm holds a big mobile franchise (about **$20B**). 

Then the plot thickens: 2016–2018 is where the story turns from hardware to *ecosystem*. NVIDIA’s CUDA momentum matters. By 2019, NVIDIA is up to about **$14.0B**, and the race is no longer just about faster chips—it’s about software support that keeps developers shipping models. Intel, meanwhile, starts paying for a long slowdown in execution—its sales climb, but confidence cracks show in the market. Intel hovers around the **$72B** range by 2019. 

2020 is the real “point-of-no-return” chapter. As AI workload demand accelerates, NVIDIA jumps to about **$18.9B**. Intel rises to around **$79B**, but the competitive gravity is shifting: AI is moving toward accelerators. In 2021, NVIDIA keeps pulling ahead to roughly **$26.9B**, while AMD makes steady progress to about **$20B**. 

2024 is when the squeeze becomes a collapse for everyone else. NVIDIA rockets to **$60B** and then to an estimated **$120B by 2025**. Intel falls hard—from about **$32B in 2024** to roughly **$30B in 2025**—while AMD climbs to about **$35B** and Qualcomm stays comparatively resilient at about **$38B**.

If this chart race felt obvious in hindsight, it’s because the turning points were real: ecosystem lock-in, data-center demand, and the shift from CPUs to accelerators.

The “AI Chip Squeeze” wasn’t just about faster hardware—it was about who owned the platform for training and inference at scale. From 2015 to 2019, NVIDIA grew from roughly $6.5B to $14.0B as CUDA and GPU-based AI workflows became the default path for developers. During the same period, Intel remained the dominant legacy player, reaching about $72.0B by 2019, while AMD and Qualcomm maintained smaller but important positions at approximately $15.0B and $26.0B respectively.

The decisive shift came in 2020–2021, when AI compute demand spiked and data-center spend accelerated. NVIDIA rose from about $18.9B in 2020 to $26.9B in 2021, while Intel peaked around $79.0B before the competitive pressure intensified. By 2022–2023, NVIDIA’s trajectory accelerated further, while Intel’s path weakened, falling to about $54.0B by 2023. 

The steepest divergence appears in 2024–2025. NVIDIA surged to about $60.0B in 2024 and reached an estimated $120.0B by 2025, reflecting the AI accelerator dominance. Intel declined to around $32.0B in 2024 and about $30.0B in 2025, while AMD climbed to ~$35.0B and Qualcomm held comparatively steadier performance near ~$38.0B.
